fields.label: Allied conduct
fields.description: Behavior/attitudes of Allied troops toward locals

fields.label: Black market
fields.description: Smuggling, theft of Allied goods, corruption, racketeering

fields.label: Bureaucracy & absurdity
fields.description: Military/administrative farce, red tape, false alarms

fields.label: Crime & banditry
fields.description: Camorra, bandits, vendettas, organized crime

fields.label: Disease & health
fields.description: Illness, hospitals, epidemics, medical matters

fields.label: Naples's character
fields.description: Naples's social fabric, class, theatricality, daily life/customs

fields.label: Personal reflection
fields.description: Lewis's own introspection, changing perspective, mood

fields.label: Poverty & hunger
fields.description: Famine, scavenging, destitution, makeshift survival

fields.label: Sex & relationships
fields.description: Prostitution, romance, marriage vetting, wartime liaisons

fields.label: Superstition & religion
fields.description: Miracles, saints, folk magic, the evil eye, ritual

fields.label: War & violence
fields.description: Combat, bombing, casualties, atrocities, military operations

fields.name: Salerno
fields.description: Salerno is a city and comune in Campania, southern Italy, and the capital of the province of the same name. With 125,958 inhabitants as of 2025, it is the second most populous municipality in the region after Naples. The city lies on the Gulf of Salerno, on the Tyrrhenian Sea.
fields.book_role: The invasion beachhead where the book opens. Lewis lands nearby in September 1943 into chaos — a German counter-attack, gas scares, rumours the beachhead will be abandoned — and the town stays a reference point for the campaign's uncertain first weeks.

fields.name: Oran
fields.description: Oran is a major coastal city located in the northwest of Algeria. It is considered the second most important city of Algeria, after the capital, Algiers, because of its population and commercial, industrial and cultural importance. It is 432 km (268 mi) west-southwest from Algiers.
fields.book_role: The Algerian port from which the section shipped to Italy; Captain Cartwright, hurt in a crash before embarkation, is left behind in hospital there as the book opens.

fields.name: Paestum
fields.description: Paestum was a major ancient Greek city on the coast of the Tyrrhenian Sea, in Magna Graecia. The ruins of Paestum are famous for their three ancient Greek temples in the Doric order dating from about 550 to 450 BCE that are in an excellent state of preservation. The city walls and amphitheatre are largely intact, and the bottom of the walls of many other structures remain, as well as paved roads.
fields.book_role: The Greek temples beside the landing beach, where the leaderless section spends its first rudderless days in Italy amid dead soldiers, and later the pointless idle life of the beachhead.

fields.name: Pompeii
fields.description: Pompeii was a city in what is now the municipality of Pompei, near Naples, in the Campania region of Italy. Along with Herculaneum, Stabiae, and many surrounding villas, it was buried under 4 to 6 m of volcanic ash and pumice in the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 AD.
fields.book_role: Invoked again and again as the template for catastrophe: a soldier gives Lewis a scrap of a Pompeii Madonna's mantle as a charm, and during the eruption he sees people frozen in the ash in the postures of the bodies at Pompeii.

fields.name: Sele river
fields.book_role: The river by the Salerno beachhead, where HQ sits through the tense, underdefended first days and the night battles of September 1943.

fields.name: Albanella
fields.description: Albanella is a town and municipality in the province of Salerno in the Campania region of south-western Italy. It is 51 kilometres (32 mi) from the city of Salerno.
fields.book_role: The rail station just south of the Sele where Fifth Army HQ — and the parasitically attached section — sits during the battle for the beachhead; German tanks push toward it to within a mile of Lewis's slit trench.

fields.name: Battipaglia
fields.description: Battipaglia is a town and comune in the Province of Salerno, in the Campania region of southern Italy. With around 50,000 inhabitants, it is one of the most populous municipalities in the province after Salerno itself, and the main agricultural, industrial and railway hub of the Sele Plain.
fields.book_role: Seen only in ruins — carpet-bombed by the Allies — as Lewis hitches back toward liberated Naples: an early measure of the destruction visited on Italian towns on mere suspicion.

fields.name: Sicily
fields.description: Sicily, officially the Sicilian Region, is an island in the central Mediterranean Sea and one of the twenty regions of Italy, situated south of the Italian Peninsula in continental Europe. With over 4.7 million inhabitants, including 1.2 million in and around the capital city of Palermo, it is both the largest and most populous island in the Mediterranean Sea.
fields.book_role: Referred to as the campaign's starting point and, more often, as shorthand for the deep-rooted world of Southern Italian banditry, landowners and assimilation that Lewis keeps coming up against.

fields.name: Calore river
fields.book_role: One of the two rivers, with the Sele, bounding the tongue of land down which German tanks advanced toward Albanella during the battle for the Salerno beachhead.

fields.name: Avellino
fields.description: Avellino is a city and comune (municipality), and capital of the province of Avellino in the region of Campania in southern Italy. It is situated in a plain surrounded by mountains 47 kilometres (29 mi) east of Naples and is an important hub on the road from Salerno to Benevento. It has 51,819 inhabitants.
fields.book_role: An inland town on the roads Lewis travels, appearing around the September 1943 fighting and again during the 1944 bandit troubles.

fields.name: Castello Castelluccia
fields.book_role: A village near the Paestum beachhead where flashing night lights are reported; investigating them is the section's first real task since landing in Italy.

fields.name: Resina
fields.description: Ercolano is a city and comune (municipality) in the Metropolitan City of Naples in the region of Campania in southern Italy. It lies at the western foot of Mount Vesuvius, on the Gulf of Naples, just southeast of Naples. It has 49,179 inhabitants.
fields.book_role: One of the towns below Vesuvius on Lewis's beat, passed through on the road back to Naples and again during the eruption.

fields.name: Sorrento
fields.description: Sorrento, officially Comune di Sorrento is a city and comune overlooking the Bay of Naples in Southern Italy. A popular tourist destination, Sorrento is located on the Sorrentine Peninsula at the southern terminus of a main branch of the Circumvesuviana rail network, within easy access from Naples and Pompei. The city is widely known for its small ceramics, lacework and marquetry (woodwork) shops.
fields.book_role: One of the Bay towns at the edge of Lewis's world, passed through on the way to and from Naples and associated with the more comfortable, touristic side of the coast.

fields.name: Torre Annunziata
fields.description: Torre Annunziata is a comune (municipality) in the Metropolitan City of Naples, in the Italian region of Campania. It is located on the Gulf of Naples, at the foot of Mount Vesuvius.
fields.book_role: A grim coastal town south of Naples where thirty-five operational maps for the Anzio landing are found on a warehouse floor, being carried off by civilians for firewood.

fields.name: Altavilla Silentina
fields.description: Altavilla Silentina is a town and comune located in the province of Salerno, Campania, some 100 km south of Naples, Italy.
fields.book_role: A hill town near Battipaglia that Lewis learns was shelled to rubble on the mere suspicion that it held Germans — an early instance of the campaign's casual destruction of Italian towns.

fields.name: Portici
fields.description: Portici is a city and comune (municipality) of the Metropolitan City of Naples in the region of Campania in southern Italy. It has 51,213 inhabitants.
fields.book_role: One of the grimy industrial towns fused into a twelve-mile suburb along the coast south of Naples, and — with Torre del Greco — an area especially exposed to Vesuvius, with fears for its military installations during the 1944 eruption.

fields.name: Nola
fields.description: Nola is a city and comune in the Metropolitan City of Naples, Campania, southern Italy. It lies on the plain between Mount Vesuvius and the Apennines. It is traditionally credited as the diocese that introduced bells to Christian worship.
fields.book_role: Appears mainly through its Feast of the Lily, whose towering ceremonial structures and procession foul the army's telephone lines — one of the book's set-piece collisions between folk ritual and the occupying army.

fields.name: Palace of the Princes of Satriano
fields.book_role: The requisitioned palace on the Riviera di Chiaia, at the Piazza Vittoria end of the seafront, where the section is billeted for most of Lewis's time in Naples.

fields.name: Piazza Vittoria
fields.book_role: The square at the Riviera di Chiaia end of the seafront where the section's requisitioned palace stands.

fields.name: Questura (Naples police HQ)
fields.book_role: Naples police headquarters, where Lewis liaises with the Italian police — on denunciation cases and the messy business of wartime romances.

fields.name: Riviera di Chiaia
fields.description: The Riviera di Chiaia is a long street in the Italian city of Naples, running along the coast of the Gulf of Naples.
fields.book_role: The seafront street where the section takes over a grand requisitioned palazzo. Lewis's Sunday observations here — aristocratic grandeur mixed with teeming working-class street life — are among the book's fondest passages.

fields.name: Afragola
fields.description: Afragola is a city and comune (municipality) in the Metropolitan City of Naples in the region of Campania in southern Italy. It has 61,581 inhabitants.
fields.book_role: One of the small towns ringing Naples that Lewis polices, standing in for the poor, Camorra-shadowed hinterland just beyond the city. It recurs around denunciations, vendettas, wire-theft prosecutions and the bandit Domenico ‘Lupo’.

fields.name: Santa Lucia (Naples)
fields.book_role: The old waterfront district, seen at its most desperate (people scavenging limpets and offal) and its most devastated, when Lewis walks through the aftermath of a bombing raid among dead children and grieving families.

fields.name: Rome
fields.description: Rome is the capital city and most populated comune (municipality) of Italy. It is also the administrative centre of the Lazio region and of the Metropolitan City of Rome. A special comune named Roma Capitale with a population of 2.7 million in an area of 1,287.36 km2 (497.1 mi2), Rome is the third most populous city in the European Union by population within city limits.
fields.book_role: Mostly referred to rather than visited: ‘the fall of Rome’, an internee escorted there for interrogation, Lattarullo's funeral-mourning trade reviving once the city falls. It marks the war moving north, away from Naples.

fields.name: San Gennaro catacombs
fields.book_role: The early-Christian catacombs entered from behind the church of San Gennaro; a fifty-strong joint force of Italian police, American counter-intelligence and the section is sent down to search them during an October 1943 spy scare.

fields.name: Bari
fields.description: Bari is the capital city of the Metropolitan City of Bari and of the region of Apulia, on the Adriatic Sea in southern Italy. It is one of the most important economic centres of mainland southern Italy. It is a port and university city as well as the city of Saint Nicholas.
fields.book_role: A rear-area town to the east, mentioned only in passing — a place a returning colleague travels through, and the kind of ordinary city that Lattarullo's fictitious funeral 'uncle' is never allowed to come from (it always has to be Rome).

fields.name: Taranto
fields.description: Taranto, historically also called Tarent in English, is a coastal city in Apulia, Southern Italy. It is the capital of the province of Taranto, serving as an important commercial port as well as the main base of the Italian navy. With a population of 185,909 as of 2025, Taranto is the second-largest city in Apulia.
fields.book_role: The eastern port: the place Lattarullo's imaginary 'uncle from Rome' pointedly never comes from, and, at the end, the port where Lewis embarks on the ship taking him away from Naples for good.

fields.name: Bar Vittoria
fields.book_role: The bar next door to the section's office where Lewis takes the newly-met Lattarullo for a marsala all'uovo — the encounter that begins their long association.

fields.name: Castel Nuovo
fields.description: Castel Nuovo, often called Maschio Angioino, is a medieval castle located in front of Piazza Municipio and the city hall in central Naples, Campania, Italy. Its scenic location and imposing size makes the castle, first erected in 1279, one of the main architectural landmarks of the city. It was a royal seat for kings of Naples, Aragon and Spain until 1815.
fields.book_role: The medieval castle on the seafront; Lewis is riding toward it along the bomb-damaged Via Partenope when he is nearly caught by one of the German delayed-action mine explosions.

fields.name: Porta Capuana
fields.description: The Porta Capuana is a Renaissance city gate in Naples, Italy, originally passing through the medieval city walls, of which two bastions remain to the sides. The gate also gives its name to the zone, which is one of the ten boroughs of Naples. This zone being part of the Fourth Municipality.
fields.book_role: The city gate by the courts of Castel Capuano, appearing around scenes of sudden street explosions and chaotic wartime justice.

fields.name: Via Partenope
fields.book_role: The bomb-damaged seafront road where Lewis has a narrow escape on his motorcycle, passing the Central Post Office minutes before one of the German delayed-action mines detonates.

fields.name: Aversa
fields.description: Aversa is a city and comune in the Province of Caserta in Campania, southern Italy, about 24 km north of Naples. It is the centre of an agricultural district, the Agro Aversano, producing wine and cheese. Aversa is also the main seat of the faculties of Architecture and Engineering of the Università degli studi della Campania "L.
fields.book_role: One of the towns north of Naples in Lewis's patch, recurring with famine-driven crime, impoverished nobility and village denunciations.

fields.name: Fontanelle (Naples)
fields.book_role: One of the heights above Naples — with the Vomero and the Observatory — to which the whole population is ordered to flee during the false delayed-mine evacuation of October 1943.

fields.name: Vomero (Naples)
fields.description: Vomero is a hilltop quarter of Naples, Italy — comprising approximately two square kilometres (0.77 sq mi) and a population of 48,000.
fields.book_role: The hilltop quarter, associated with the section's informant network and with several intelligence flaps — the false-mine mass evacuation, the traced Anzio leak.

fields.name: Philippeville
fields.description: Skikda is a city in northeastern Algeria and a port on the Mediterranean. It is the capital of Skikda Province and Skikda District.
fields.book_role: The Algerian town whose notorious prison pit — where dissidents were flung into total darkness — is the only jail Lewis has known before he is sent into Poggio Reale.

fields.name: Poggio Reale prison
fields.book_role: The prison and its courts, where Lewis's cases keep ending up — a German held over the mine hoax, the well-connected racketeer Fortuna expecting acquittal, petty thieves tried within sight of an open black market. It embodies the book's sense of justice falling only on the powerless.

fields.name: Posillipo (Naples)
fields.description: Posillipo is an affluent residential quarter of Naples, southern Italy, located along the northern coast of the Gulf of Naples.
fields.book_role: The headland across the bay where, Lewis notes, Pliny watched the eruption that buried Pompeii — and where Lewis himself stands to watch Vesuvius erupt in 1944.

fields.name: Filangieri prison
fields.book_role: The Naples women's prison the section is repeatedly ordered to deliver women to on flimsy or political charges — a German-born wife, a woman the partisans had jailed — with frantic last-minute collections of warm clothing for those sent into its cold.

fields.name: Vico Chiatamone
fields.book_role: A lane near the seafront, partly blocked by a collapsed building, where a sanitary post is set up during the typhus scare and every passer-by is dusted with anti-typhus powder.

fields.name: San Carlo opera house
fields.description: The Real Teatro di San Carlo, as originally named by the Bourbon monarchy but today known simply as the Teatro (di) San Carlo, is a historic opera house in Naples, Italy, connected to the Royal Palace and adjacent to the Piazza del Plebiscito. It is the oldest continuously active venue for opera in the world, having opened in 1737, decades before either Milan's La Scala or Venice's La Fenice.
fields.book_role: The opera house where Naples's social life is really conducted; in the book it becomes an emblem of the black market, its reopening-night audience of upper-class women all wearing coats cut from stolen Allied blankets.

fields.name: Via Chiaia
fields.book_role: Once the resort of the town's aristocracy, now lined with vast dark half-empty palazzi; Lewis's impoverished-noble contacts Losurdo and Mosca live here, and a marriage candidate's flat nearby gives her away by the fortune in black-market soap in the kitchen.

fields.name: Via San Felice
fields.book_role: The street of Lattarullo's flat, where he serves the improbably lavish borrowed-furniture lunch.

fields.name: Vesuvius
fields.description: Mount Vesuvius is a somma–stratovolcano located on the Gulf of Naples in Campania, Italy, about 9 km (5.6 mi) east of Naples and a short distance from the shore. It is one of several volcanoes forming the Campanian volcanic arc. Vesuvius consists of a large cone partially encircled by the steep rim of a summit caldera, resulting from the collapse of an earlier, much higher structure.
fields.book_role: Dominates March 1944, when the volcano erupts spectacularly — Lewis reaches for Pliny's account of Pompeii — burying nearby towns in ash while he consults seismologists about the risk to military installations.

fields.name: Acerra
fields.description: Acerra is a city and comune (municipality) in the Metropolitan City of Naples in the region of Campania, southern Italy, about 15 kilometres northeast of the capital in Naples. It has 58,585 inhabitants.
fields.book_role: One of the ring of towns north of Naples put under Lewis's security charge (with Casoria, Afragola and Aversa), all of them, he discovers, inside Camorra territory. He calls on its skeleton Carabinieri force and vets a local girl hoping to marry a British guardsman.

fields.name: Casoria
fields.description: Casoria is a city and comune (municipality) in the Metropolitan City of Naples in the region of Campania in southern Italy, located about 5 kilometres northeast of Naples. It has 73,257 inhabitants.
fields.book_role: Another of the poor towns north of Naples that Lewis polices, tied to the fruitless wire-theft investigation and the wider Camorra-country cases.

fields.name: San Pasquale (church & district)
fields.book_role: A self-contained little community with its own festivals and feuds around the church of San Pasquale, which holds the preserved body of the Blessed Egideo, protector of pregnant women; Lewis reaches it down the Via Carducci.

fields.name: Via Carducci
fields.book_role: A street running down to the Riviera di Chiaia near the section's HQ; Lewis follows it into the square of the church of San Pasquale and notes a house there locally shunned as unlucky.

fields.name: Calabritto Palace
fields.book_role: The palace directly across from the section's headquarters windows; Lewis watches its courtyard life at close range and, on his last day in Naples, takes a long farewell look at its huge guardian statues.

fields.name: Villa Nazionale
fields.book_role: The seafront park on the Riviera di Chiaia — a backdrop for Sunday crowds, the arrival of spring, and later the mob attacks on women seen with Allied soldiers.

fields.name: Torrito
fields.book_role: A village near Aversa ruled 'with a rod of iron' by the corrupt Marshal Benvenuto, a recurring name in unit complaints; Lewis also goes there to hear the partisan leader Albano's account of an SS reprisal massacre that has left the whole village in mourning.

fields.name: Caivano
fields.description: Caivano is a comune (municipality) in the Metropolitan City of Naples in the Italian region Campania, located about 14 km (8.7 mi) northeast of Naples.
fields.book_role: One of the Camorra-zone towns north of Naples in Lewis's security patch, recurring with denunciation cases, the eccentric landowner ‘La Pitonessa’, and the bandit ‘Lupo’.

fields.name: Zona di Camorra
fields.book_role: Lewis's own name for the belt of towns north of Naples he is given to police: ‘unknowingly located deep in Camorra territory’, picturesque on the surface, poor and criminally governed underneath.

fields.name: Forcella (market district)
fields.book_role: The market quarter synonymous with the black market — stolen Allied goods sold openly, almost elegantly, a short walk from the courts trying petty thieves.

fields.name: Via Forcella
fields.book_role: The street through the Forcella market, recurring with the wire-theft case and the open trade in stolen Allied goods.

fields.name: Matlock
fields.book_role: Not in Italy at all — the site of the Field Security training course in England, which Lewis keeps measuring the messy reality of Naples against; a drunken security leak he investigates is exactly the textbook case the course had warned of.

fields.name: Via Filippo Palizzi
fields.book_role: A Vomero street where Lewis's friends Alberto and Norah live; dropping in on them of an evening becomes his habitual refuge, a friendship he hopes will outlast the war.

fields.name: Castel Capuano
fields.description: Castel Capuano is a castle in Naples, southern Italy. It takes its name from the fact that it was at that point in the city walls where the road led out to the city of Capua. The castle is at the southwest end of via dei Tribunali, and until recently housed the Naples Hall of Justice, which has now moved to the new Civic Center, the Centro Direzionale.
fields.book_role: The old castle housing Naples's courts, where Lewis watches wartime justice at its most arbitrary — smuggling trials collapsing through incompetence, punishment landing only on the weak.

fields.name: Castellammare di Stabia
fields.description: Castellammare di Stabia is a city and comune (municipality) in the Metropolitan City of Naples in the region of Campania in southern Italy. It is situated on the Bay of Naples about 30 km (19 mi) southeast of Naples, on the route to Sorrento. It has 61,937 inhabitants.

fields.name: Agropoli
fields.description: Agropoli is a town and comune located in the Cilento area of the province of Salerno, Campania, Italy. It is situated at the start of the Cilentan Coast, on the Tyrrhenian Sea.
fields.book_role: A coastal town south of Salerno cited in the newspapers' gleeful catalogue of audacious wartime thefts — here, small ships lifted bodily out of the water and spirited away.

fields.name: Piazza Dante
fields.description: Piazza Dante is a large public square in Naples, Italy, named after the medieval poet Dante Alighieri. The square is dominated by a 19th-century statue of Dante, sculpted by Tito Angelini.
fields.book_role: The square at the top of the Via Roma that Lewis uses to measure the city's mental distance from the countryside — its cafés are ten miles and a thousand years from the Bronze-Age world of Afragola. Its Café Savoia is a haunt of line-crossers, and an old woman stops him near here trying to sell her daughter.

fields.name: Procida
fields.description: Procida is one of the Phlegraean Islands off the coast of Naples in southern Italy. The island is between Cape Miseno and the island of Ischia. With its tiny satellite island of Vivara, it is a comune (municipality) of the Metropolitan City of Naples, in the region of Campania.
fields.book_role: The prison island of which 'little but blood-chilling legends' is known, the destination of lifers and of the petty thieves who fill its cells while well-connected racketeers walk free — the book's recurring image of one-sided justice.

fields.name: Caserta
fields.description: Caserta is the capital of the province of Caserta in the Campania region of Italy. An important agricultural, commercial, and industrial comune and city, Caserta is located 36 kilometres north of Naples on the edge of the Campanian plain at the foot of the Campanian Subapennine mountain range. The city is best known for the 18th-century Bourbon Royal Palace of Caserta.
fields.book_role: Everyone visits it for its royal palace, but for Lewis it mainly marks distance: the road to it runs right past Afragola, yet Afragola's vendetta world stays, for Neapolitans, a thousand miles away. It is also a target for the Lupo band's train hijackings.

fields.name: Via San Pasquale
fields.book_role: A Chiaia street where Lewis sees his first pazzariello — the costumed 'joker' hired to advertise a reopening shop — among stalls now also selling looted American cigarettes.

fields.name: Vico Satriano
fields.book_role: The narrow street overlooked by one side of the section's building; Lewis reads its noise and bustle as a barometer of the city's returning life as spring arrives.

fields.name: Capri
fields.description: Capri is an island located in the Tyrrhenian Sea off the Sorrento Peninsula, on the south side of the Gulf of Naples in the Campania region of Italy. A resort destination since the time of the Roman Republic, it is known for its natural beauty, historic sites, and tourism industry. It has 13,451 inhabitants.
fields.book_role: The island escape — a golden, carefree boat trip with Captain Frazer and Lola stands out sharply against the war, and the island reappears through Frazer's turbulent romance.

fields.name: Via Roma
fields.description: Via Toledo is an ancient street and one of the most important shopping thoroughfares in the city of Naples, Italy. The street is almost 1.2 kilometres (0.75 mi) long and starts at Piazza Dante and ends in Piazza Trieste e Trento, near Piazza del Plebiscito.
fields.book_role: Naples's main thoroughfare, backdrop to street scenes of the black market trading openly and, at its bleakest, a mother trying to sell her daughter.

fields.name: Café Savoia
fields.book_role: A café in the Piazza Dante, a known rendezvous of 'dubious characters', where the line-crosser and A-Force guide Patierno is picked up.

fields.name: Ischia
fields.description: Ischia is a volcanic island in the Tyrrhenian Sea. It lies at the northern end of the Gulf of Naples, about 30 kilometres from the city of Naples. It is the largest of the Phlegrean Islands.
fields.book_role: The Bay island where Frazer's mistress Lola and her friend retire for the summer once the affair ends; also noted for the deep ashfall it takes during the eruption.

fields.name: San Sebastiano (town near Vesuvius)
fields.book_role: The town in the path of the 1944 lava flow, which Lewis reaches through falling ash to report on as it is threatened.

fields.name: San Giorgio (near Vesuvius)
fields.description: San Giorgio a Cremano is a city and comune (municipality) in the Metropolitan City of Naples in the region of Campania in southern Italy. It is located on the foothills of Mount Vesuvius to the west of the volcano and the Tyrrhenian Sea, and is five kilometres to the south east of the centre of Naples. The municipality has views of Mount Vesuvius, Mount Somma and the Bay of Naples.
fields.book_role: San Giorgio a Cremano, below Vesuvius: during the March 1944 eruption Lewis passes its roadblock on the way to the threatened towns, and draws rations from the South Africans stationed there.

fields.name: Cercola
fields.description: Cercola is a comune (municipality) in the Metropolitan City of Naples in the Italian region of Campania, located about 9 km northeast of Naples.
fields.book_role: A town below Vesuvius reported to be threatened by the lava during the March 1944 eruption, prompting one of Lewis's on-the-spot reporting trips.

fields.name: Maddaloni Bridge
fields.book_role: Turns up in Del Giudice's San Gennaro lore: a forgotten statue of the saint erected on this bridge is said to have saved Naples when the image dredged from the sea could not be found.

fields.name: Pozzuoli
fields.description: Pozzuoli is a city and comune (municipality) in the Metropolitan City of Naples in the region of Campania in southern Italy. The main city of the Phlegrean Peninsula, it has 74,665 inhabitants.
fields.book_role: Visited on a rare day off — a town ‘strangely untouched by the war’, calmer and more foreign-feeling than the rest of the Naples area.

fields.name: Torre del Greco
fields.description: Torre del Greco is a comune (municipality) in the Metropolitan City of Naples in the region of Campania in southern Italy. It has 78,839 inhabitants.
fields.book_role: One of the coastal towns south of Naples fused into a single grim suburb; historically overwhelmed by Vesuvius's lava, it is again a focus of concern during the 1944 eruption.

fields.name: Campi Flegrei
fields.description: The Phlegraean Fields is a large volcanic caldera west of Naples, Italy. The Neapolitan Yellow Tuff eruption produced just 50 cubic kilometers. It is, however, one of relatively few volcanoes large enough to form a caldera.
fields.book_role: The volcanic area west of Naples where crowds gather in spring 1944 around a twelve-year-old visionary — a 'local Bernadette' — to whom the Virgin is said to appear.

fields.name: Pomigliano
fields.description: Pomigliano d'Arco is a municipality in the Metropolitan City of Naples in Italy, located north of Mount Vesuvius.
fields.book_role: The town of the 'flying monk', a friar who claims to have flown to rescue a downed pilot and displays the stigmata — one of the wave of wartime miracles Lewis catalogues in spring 1944.

fields.name: Marano
fields.description: Marano di Napoli is a city and comune (municipality) in the Metropolitan City of Naples in the region of Campania in southern Italy, located about 9 kilometres northwest of Naples. Partly located on the Camaldoli hill, with 57,631 inhabitants, it is one of the most populous municipalities in the metropolitan city.
fields.book_role: The town whose mayor, for lack of any other transport, arrives at a spring-1944 apparition at the Campi Flegrei in a motor-hearse.

fields.name: Castel Sant'Elmo
fields.description: Castel Sant'Elmo is a medieval fortress located on Vomero Hill adjacent to the Certosa di San Martino, overlooking Naples, Italy. The name "Sant'Elmo" derives from a former 10th-century church dedicated to Sant'Erasmo, shortened to "Ermo" and ultimately altered to "Elmo". Located near the upper terminus of the Petraio, one of the city's earliest pedestrian connections between upper and lower Naples, the fortress now serves as a museum, exhibition hall, and offices.

fields.name: Padula
fields.description: Padula is a town and comune in the province of Salerno, located in the Campania region of south-western Italy. The town is best known for the Carthusian monastery of Certosa di San Lorenzo, it is one of the largest monasteries in Italy and a notable example of Baroque architecture. The Certosa is included in the UNESCO World Heritage Site.
fields.book_role: The former monastery used as an internment camp: the writer Curzio Malaparte has been quietly released from it, and it is where the section must collect a female internee too important to be named in writing.

fields.name: Piazza Municipio
fields.book_role: The Capri square where Lewis and Frazer sit in a café on their golden day trip: a world away from Naples, escapist and make-believe.

fields.name: Villa Tiberius (Capri)
fields.book_role: Tiberius's cliff-top villa on Capri, whose 'ancient scandals' are part of the island's tourist patter; it is pointed out to Lewis on his day trip.

fields.name: Terni
fields.description: Terni is a city in the southern portion of the region of Umbria in central Italy. It is near the border with Lazio. The city is the capital of the province of Terni, located in the plain of the River Nera.
fields.book_role: A town in Umbria near which five British privates escaped a German prison camp before making their way south to Nola, where Lewis interviews them.

fields.name: Santa Maria della Colombina
fields.book_role: The town of an unusually memorable marriage vetting — of the elegant Contessa della Peruta, a striking contrast to the destitution Lewis usually meets on such errands.

fields.name: Rione Amedeo
fields.book_role: A fashionable Chiaia quarter; it appears when the infatuated Captain Frazer is pushed into illegally requisitioning an empty flat there for his mistress, Lola.

fields.name: Monte Vergine
fields.description: Sanctuary of Montevergine is a Marian church in Mercogliano, located in the hamlet of Montevergine. It's a part of the Territorial Abbey of Montevergine, one of the six Italian territorial abbeys. Inside, the painting of the Madonna di Montevergine is venerated and it is estimated that about one and a half million pilgrims visit it every year.
fields.book_role: The mountain sanctuary above Naples whose Whitsun pilgrimage is banned in 1944 to public dismay; its district also gives Lattarullo a choice tale of a millionaire woman black-marketeer.

fields.name: Monte Santangelo
fields.book_role: The cave-sanctuary of St Michael in Puglia; it appears only as the source of the venerated lump of rock that is the one treasured object, besides a royal salver, in Lattarullo's bare flat.

fields.name: Frattamaggiore
fields.description: Frattamaggiore is a comune in the Metropolitan City of Naples, Campania, Italy. It is located 15 km (9.3 mi) north of Naples and 15 km (9.3 mi) southwest of Caserta. It was awarded the title of "City of art" in 2008 and named Benedictine city in 1997.
fields.book_role: A Camorra-country town near Aversa — home of the bandit Domenico 'Lupo', and the site of one of the harsh new joint police raids on a bandit hideout that Lewis observes.

fields.name: Duomo di Napoli
fields.description: Naples Cathedral, or the Cathedral of the Assumption of Mary, is a Roman Catholic cathedral, the main church of Naples, southern Italy, and the seat of the Archbishop of Naples. It is widely known as the Cathedral of Saint Januarius, in honour of the city's patron saint.
fields.book_role: Naples Cathedral, where the blood of San Gennaro is kept; in the book it is the focus of the tense May 1944 public vigil over whether the miracle of liquefaction will occur.

fields.name: Vico Freddo
fields.book_role: The lane holding the section's 'local shrine', where the two women who clean for them go to light candles during the anxious May 1944 vigil over San Gennaro's blood.

fields.name: Patrica
fields.description: Patrica is a hill-top comune (municipality) in the Province of Frosinone in the Italian region Lazio.
fields.book_role: One of the southern-Lazio villages where Lewis reports every woman was raped by French colonial troops in May 1944.

fields.name: Pofi
fields.description: Pofi is a comune (municipality) of about 4,200 inhabitants in the province of Frosinone in the Italian region Lazio, located about 80 kilometres (50 mi) southeast of Rome and about 9 kilometres (6 mi) southeast of Frosinone.
fields.book_role: One of the southern-Lazio villages where Lewis reports the wholesale rape of women by French colonial troops in May 1944.

fields.name: Isoletta
fields.book_role: One of the southern-Lazio villages where, Lewis reports, every woman was raped by French colonial troops in May 1944.

fields.name: Supino
fields.description: Supino is a comune (municipality) in the Province of Frosinone in the Italian region Lazio, located about 70 kilometres (43 mi) southeast of Rome and about 10 kilometres (6 mi) west of Frosinone.
fields.book_role: One of the southern-Lazio villages where Lewis reports the wholesale rape of women by French colonial troops in May 1944.

fields.name: Morolo
fields.description: Morolo is a comune (municipality) in the Province of Frosinone in the Italian region Lazio, located about 70 kilometres (43 mi) southeast of Rome and about 12 kilometres (7 mi) west of Frosinone.
fields.book_role: One of the southern-Lazio villages where Lewis reports the wholesale rape of women by French colonial troops in May 1944.

fields.name: Lenola
fields.book_role: A southern-Lazio town that fell to the Allies on 21 May 1944; Lewis records the mass rape of its women by Moroccan troops that followed.

fields.name: Castro dei Volsci
fields.description: Castro dei Volsci is a comune (municipality) in the Province of Frosinone in the Italian region Lazio, located about 90 kilometres (56 mi) southeast of Rome and about 14 kilometres (9 mi) southeast of Frosinone. It takes its name from the Latin word Castrum and the Volsci, who lived here in ancient times.
fields.book_role: A southern-Lazio town where, Lewis records, doctors treated three hundred victims of rape after French colonial troops passed through in May 1944.

fields.name: Ceccano
fields.description: Ceccano is a town and comune in the province of Frosinone, Lazio, central Italy, in the Latin Valley.
fields.book_role: One of the southern-Lazio towns overrun by French colonial troops in May 1944; Lewis records that the British had to build a guarded camp there to protect Italian women from mass rape.

fields.name: Santa Maria a Vico
fields.book_role: One of the towns near Afragola terrorised by deserting Moroccan troops in mid-1944; Lewis goes there to see a girl driven insane by a gang rape.

fields.name: Via Gravina
fields.book_role: The street where the Communist leader Eugenio Reale keeps a flat; Lewis visits him half a dozen times but concludes the calls yield less than a single meeting with Lattarullo.

fields.name: Cancello
fields.book_role: A village near which five Moroccan soldiers are lured into a house and poisoned in revenge for atrocities; also the field hospital where the captured saboteur Salvatore Loreto turns up.

fields.name: Guardia Sanframondi
fields.description: Guardia Sanframondi is a town and comune in the Province of Benevento, in Campania region, in Italy. It is best known for its wine production, the wine festival Vinalia and for its Christian penitential rite held every seven years.
fields.book_role: The town of a revived, medieval-style flagellant procession, recounted to Lewis by a colleague as one of a run of extreme feast-day spectacles in the Beneventano.

fields.name: Amalfi
fields.description: Amalfi is a town and comune in the province of Salerno, in the region of Campania, Italy, on the Gulf of Salerno. It lies at the mouth of a deep ravine, at the foot of Monte Cerreto, surrounded by dramatic cliffs and coastal scenery. The town of Amalfi was the capital of the maritime republic known as the Duchy of Amalfi, an important trading power in the Mediterranean between 839 and around 1200.
fields.book_role: Appears once, when Lewis drives the folklore writer Del Giudice there to see the thrice-yearly liquefaction of the 'manna' relic of St Andrew — one of the book's studies of Neapolitan religious spectacle.

fields.name: Monte Nuovo
fields.description: Monte Nuovo is a cinder cone volcano within the Campi Flegrei caldera, near Naples, southern Italy. A series of damaging earthquakes and changes in land elevation preceded its only eruption, during the most recent part of the Holocene, which lasted from September 29 to October 6, 1538, when it was formed. The event is important in the history of science because it was the first eruption in modern times to be described by a large number of witnesses.
fields.book_role: A small volcano near Pozzuoli that rose overnight in 1538 — part of the dense layering of ruin and legend Lewis dwells on during his tourist day around the Phlegraean Fields.

fields.name: Mondragone
fields.description: Mondragone is a comune or municipality in the Province of Caserta in the Italian region of Campania. It is located about 45 kilometres (28 mi) northwest of Naples and about 40 kilometres (25 mi) west of Caserta. It faces mountains on one side and ocean on the other, with the former lending it a reputation for game birds such as quail.
fields.book_role: A Camorra town on the coast north of Naples; Lewis notes it as the narrow corridor by which the 'secret tribal life' of the Camorra zone reaches the sea.

fields.name: Baia
fields.description: Baiae is an ancient Roman town situated on the northwest shore of the Gulf of Naples and now in the comune of Bacoli. It was a resort for centuries in antiquity, particularly towards the end of the Roman Republic, when it was reckoned as superior to Capri, Pompeii, and Herculaneum by wealthy Romans, who built villas here from 100 BC. Ancient authors attest that many emperors built in Baia, almost in competition with their predecessors, and they and their courts often stayed there.
fields.book_role: One of the ancient pleasure-towns on the bay past Pozzuoli, outside the Camorra zone; Lewis visits on his rare tourist day off and dwells on its Roman history of luxury and vice.

fields.name: Capodichino airport
fields.description: Naples-Capodichino International Airport is the international airport serving Naples, its metropolitan city and the Campania region. Located 3.2 NM north-northeast of the city in Naples, within the Capodichino area of the San Pietro a Patierno district, the airport is officially named Aeroporto di Napoli-Capodichino Ugo Niutta, after decorated WWI pilot Ugo Niutta.
fields.book_role: Naples's airport; Lewis goes there to collect an Italian general said to have been drugged and kidnapped — one of the 'Maugham-ish' episodes of his intelligence work.

fields.name: Algeria
fields.description: Algeria, officially the People's Democratic Republic of Algeria, is a country in the Maghreb region of North Africa. Spanning over 2,381,741 square kilometres (919,595 sq mi), it is the largest country in Africa and the tenth largest in the world. It is bordered to the northeast by Tunisia; to the east by Libya; to the southeast by Niger; to the southwest by Mali, Mauritania, and Western Sahara; to the west by Morocco; and to the north by the Mediterranean Sea.
fields.book_role: Where Lewis served before Italy; it surfaces only in memory, when he unexpectedly finds a nurse he had known there running the hospital ward holding a captured Italian saboteur.

fields.name: Altamura
fields.description: Altamura is a town and comune of Apulia, in southern Italy. It is located on one of the hills of the Murge plateau in the Metropolitan City of Bari, 45 kilometres southwest of Bari, close to the border with Basilicata. As of 2017, it has a population to 70,595.

fields.name: Benevento
fields.description: Benevento is a city and comune (municipality) of Campania, Italy, capital of the province of Benevento. It is situated on a hill 130 metres above sea level at the confluence of the Calore Irpino and the Sabato. As of June 30, 2025, Benevento has 55,319 inhabitants.
fields.book_role: Where Lewis is posted, alone, in August 1944 to run security for a city wrecked by an air raid and sunk in near-universal mourning. His weeks here are dominated by typhus and typhoid, the arrival of undisciplined Canadian troops, and an escalating, dangerous campaign against motorised bandits.

fields.name: Hotel Vesuvio (Benevento)
fields.book_role: The damaged, stripped-out hotel where Lewis lodges during the Benevento posting.

fields.name: Sagranella
fields.book_role: The remote hill village — with its ‘strange local fox-cult ritual’ — where the section relocates after Don Ubaldo's death in September 1944, and where Lewis realises with unease that locals take him for a jettatore.

fields.name: San Marco di Cavali
fields.book_role: A hill village in the Monti del Sannio where a fringe right-wing movement — led by a self-styled reincarnation of Garibaldi — holds a rally that Lewis is sent to report on.

fields.name: Monti del Sannio
fields.book_role: The mountains around Benevento; Lewis drives thirty miles into them, to the hill village of San Marco di Cavali, to report on a fringe right-wing rally.

fields.name: Campobasso
fields.description: Campobasso is a city and comune (municipality) in southern Italy, the capital of the region of Molise and of the province of Campobasso. It is located in the high basin of the Biferno river, surrounded by the Sannio and Matese mountains. It has 47,399 inhabitants.
fields.book_role: Appears once, as the town to whose hospital the reckless Canadians dump an Italian civilian they have run over and nearly killed.

fields.name: Café Roma (Benevento)
fields.book_role: The Benevento café outside which a man is shot dead with a lupara one morning; by the time Lewis arrives the body has vanished and no passer-by or waiter will admit to seeing anything — his sharpest picture of the town's wall of fear.

fields.name: Ufita river
fields.book_role: A river just outside Benevento where the bridge is down; Lewis picks the lonely road across it as the site of a night checkpoint against bandit traffic in September 1944.

fields.name: Corso Umberto
fields.book_role: The Benevento street where Irene Imbrosi has a flat in a block where 'men of substance' keep their mistresses; Lewis interviews her there about a rape by an unidentified Allied soldier.

fields.name: Tunisia
fields.description: Tunisia, officially the Republic of Tunisia, is a country in the Maghreb region of North Africa. It is bordered by Algeria to the west and southwest, Libya to the southeast, and the Mediterranean Sea to the north and east. Tunisia also shares maritime borders with Italy through the islands of Sicily and Sardinia to the north and Malta to the east.
fields.book_role: Where Lewis parted from his colleague Neil Armstrong eighteen months earlier; their September 1944 reunion, after Armstrong has been through the whole campaign, prompts reflection on how the war and the south change a man.

fields.name: Lago di Patria
fields.book_role: A coastal lagoon west of Naples where Lewis joins Ingegnere Crespi's family on a Sunday outing to gather mushrooms and salad plants and shoot at migrant birds.

fields.name: Via Aniello Falcone
fields.book_role: A panoramic Vomero street; it appears as the address of one of the many women Lewis is sent to vet for marriage to British soldiers.

fields.name: Via Calabritto
fields.book_role: The street below the section's first-floor HQ windows — near enough that a courtly contact can hold a conversation with someone in it purely by movements of the head and hands.

fields.name: Villa Floridiana
fields.description: The Villa Floridiana is a monumental house located amid a large park in the Vomero quarter in Naples, southern Italy. It overlooks the western Neapolitan suburbs of Chiaia and Mergellina.
fields.book_role: The villa and park on the Vomero whose terrace commands the great panoramic view over Naples — the last sight Lewis knows he won't have time for before he leaves.

fields.name: Port Said
fields.description: Port Said is a port city that lies in northeast Egypt extending about 30 km (19 mi) along the coast of the Mediterranean Sea, straddling the west bank of the northern mouth of the Suez Canal. The city is the capital of the Port Said Governorate and forms the majority of the governorate, comprising seven of the governorate's eight administrative regions. In 2024, it had a population of 790,000 people.
fields.book_role: The Egyptian port where Lewis is to embark three thousand Russian ex-POWs for repatriation — the assignment that ends his time in Naples.

fields.name: Persian Gulf
fields.description: The Persian Gulf, sometimes called the Arabian Gulf, is a mediterranean sea in West Asia. The body of water is an extension of the Arabian Sea and the larger Indian Ocean located between the Arabian Peninsula and Iran (Persia). It is connected to the Gulf of Oman in the east by the Strait of Hormuz.
fields.book_role: Part of the route of Lewis's abrupt final assignment — repatriating Russian ex-POWs from Port Said via the Red Sea, the Persian Gulf and Iran — with which the book ends.

fields.name: Red Sea
fields.description: The Red Sea is a mediterranean sea lying between the Arabian Peninsula and Africa. It is an inlet of the Indian Ocean. Its connection to the ocean is in the south, through the Bab-el-Mandeb Strait and the Gulf of Aden.
fields.book_role: Part of the route of Lewis's final assignment, repatriating Russian ex-POWs from Port Said toward the Soviet Union — the journey on which the book closes.

fields.name: Khorramshahr
fields.description: Khorramshahr is a city in the Central District of Khorramshahr County, Khuzestan province, Iran, serving as capital of both the county and the district.
fields.book_role: The Iranian port that is the endpoint of Lewis's final assignment repatriating Russian ex-POWs — the last place named in the book.

fields.name: Captain Cartwright
fields.description: The section's Field Security Officer.
fields.book_role: Smashed up in a car crash the day before embarkation and left in hospital in Oran, so the section lands in Italy leaderless; when he finally reaches them, his face 'covered with plaster', it is to admit that their presence at Paestum serves 'no purpose of any kind'.

fields.name: Sergeant-Major Dashwood
fields.description: The section's warrant officer. (Same man as 'Sergeant-Major (John) Dashwood'.)
fields.book_role: In the confusion after the landing, decides to send four of the section by motorcycle along the shore to Salerno in the hope of finding the Field Security Officer and an order releasing them from their 'absurd predicament'.

fields.name: Moore
fields.description: One of the section's sergeants.
fields.book_role: Makes a hair-raising twelve-mile jeep dash out of the Salerno battle to rejoin the section; a year later he is 'working on with unabated vigour' despite hepatitis — part of the section's slow grinding-down by illness.

fields.name: Robert Parkinson
fields.description: A section member — 'that investigatory tiger' — who handles Lewis's doctor contacts.
fields.book_role: Works for weeks with Placella to shut down the Pace Hospital's certificate racket; when Lewis is manoeuvred off a marriage vetting, it is Parkinson who is sent to do it instead.

fields.name: Evans
fields.description: A member of Lewis's Field Security section.
fields.book_role: One of the four men left to police Naples itself; he and Lewis are sent to ransack the silk-lined apartment of Prince Pignatelli, arrested for espionage.

fields.name: Durham
fields.description: A member of Lewis's Field Security section, one of only four left to cover Naples itself. (Same man as 'Bernard Durham'.)
fields.book_role: Among the handful of section men — with Parkinson, Evans and Lewis — holding the city after the rest were dispersed to the coast and to Nola; later wounded near Avellino.

fields.name: Eric Williams
fields.description: The section's best Italian speaker.
fields.book_role: Sent as 'a solitary exile' to run security in Nola, where the Feast of the Lily brings the town — and the army's telephone lines — to a standstill; his complaints supply one of the book's set-piece feast stories.

fields.name: Vincente Lattarullo
fields.description: One of Naples's four thousand briefless lawyers — 'distinguished, fragile-looking' and slowly starving; 'motivated', he says, 'by a passion for justice'.
fields.book_role: Lewis's 'prize acquisition' among his civilian contacts and, more than that, his window onto the city: the borrowed-furniture lunch, the sideline as a hired 'uncle from Rome' at funerals, and his complete ignorance of the vendetta country ten miles from his café all become set-pieces of the book.

fields.name: Sauro
fields.description: A young soldier — Italian father, German mother — behind the October 1943 delayed-mine hoax that emptied Naples.
fields.book_role: Sent to decide whether he should be shot as a spy, Lewis finds not a 'gigantic pale-eyed Teuton' but a small, hungry boy, and reports him mentally unbalanced to save his life.

fields.name: Signora Gentile
fields.description: A Naples woman recently released from the Filangieri gaol, where the partisans had held her on 'vague charges of collaboration'.
fields.book_role: Hosts the escapist, nostalgically frivolous dinner — Lewis's first in a civilian house — at which he meets Lola.

fields.name: Captain Frazer
fields.description: A tall, handsome RASC captain whose hands are on military supplies.
fields.book_role: Lola's lover; Lewis is roped in to interpret for the couple and becomes a bemused witness to the whole affair — the white-bread courtship, Frazer's health wrecked by Lola's demands, the golden Capri outing, the break-ups and reconciliations, and finally his posting away.

fields.name: Signora Lola
fields.description: A war widow, once the mistress of a Fascist hierarch, now Captain Frazer's lover.
fields.book_role: Asks Lewis to interpret her affair with the wordless Frazer and to settle its 'basic matters'; over the following months he follows the relationship through the Capri trip, the break-ups and suicide threats, and her retirement to Ischia 'to deflate' once Frazer is posted away.

fields.name: Sergeant-Major (John) Dashwood
fields.description: The section's warrant officer. (Also recorded here as 'Sergeant-Major Dashwood'.)
fields.book_role: Runs the section in the Field Security Officer's absence in the leaderless first weeks in Italy, and is later the bearer of unwelcome HQ news — including the cut to informant funds.

fields.name: Ingeniere Losurdo
fields.description: An impoverished Naples engineer living in genteel poverty on the Via Chiaia.
fields.book_role: One of the trio — with Mosca and Lattarullo — of unmarried, well-connected, near-destitute contacts so alike they 'could easily have been members of the same family'.

fields.name: Avvocato Mosca
fields.description: An impoverished Naples lawyer, entitled to style himself Conte but no longer bothering.
fields.book_role: One of the trio of genteel-poor bachelor contacts — with Losurdo and Lattarullo — whose grand, mouldering, half-empty palazzi on the Via Chiaia become Lewis's picture of the ruined Neapolitan gentry.

fields.name: Prince A.
fields.description: The head of a leading Neapolitan noble family, an absentee landlord and enthusiastic informant.
fields.book_role: Calls at HQ with his sister Luisa to ask, with complete composure, whether she might enter an army brothel.

fields.name: Luisa
fields.description: The sister of the informant Prince A.
fields.book_role: On the visit when her brother asks whether she might be admitted to a (nonexistent) British army brothel, she takes the refusal with the same 'polite calm' — a small scene of the era's blunt calculus of sex and survival.

fields.name: Professore Placella
fields.description: A Naples gynaecologist whose speciality is the surgical restoration of virginity — his replacement, he boasts, is better than the original.
fields.book_role: Parkinson's most valuable medical contact; he helps expose the hospital racket by which syphilitic prostitutes bought clean bills of health, and later helps spring the trap on the coercive VD round-up.

fields.name: Albano
fields.description: The partisan leader of Torrito, a village near Aversa.
fields.book_role: Lewis reluctantly travels to Torrito to hear his account of the 'heroic four days' of the September 1943 uprising and the SS reprisal that followed — a massacre that has left the whole village in mourning. He finds Albano a haggard, haunted man who speaks very quietly, as if afraid of being overheard.

fields.name: Vito Genovese
fields.description: Vito Genovese was an Italian-born American mafioso and the boss of the Genovese crime family of New York City. A childhood friend and criminal associate of Lucky Luciano, Genovese took part in the Castellammarese War and helped Luciano shape the Mafia's rise as a major force in organized crime in the United States. He would later lead Luciano's crime family, which was renamed by the FBI after Genovese in 1957.
fields.book_role: Born near Naples, the exiled American mafia boss has taken a job as an AMG interpreter and manoeuvred himself into 'unassailable power' in the military government; the new mayors of the Camorra-zone towns are said to be his nominees, and the black market runs under his protection.

fields.name: Donna Maria Fidora ('La Pitonessa')
fields.description: The richest landowner near Caivano, a former circus performer who had wrestled a python — hence 'La Pitonessa'.
fields.book_role: Lewis's first contact inside the Camorra zone outside the police; barred as a woman from the Camorra itself but a valuable informant, she runs her late husband's estate with professional efficiency and turns up, incongruously, at Lewis's hospital bedside.

fields.name: Norah Gemelli
fields.description: A Naples neighbour of the arrested Signora Esposito-Lau, with an Irish mother and perfect English; she reads Dante and Leopardi aloud.
fields.book_role: The centre of the circle of friends Lewis makes and treasures — and, at a dinner, the source of the true Anzio-landing leak he is then ordered to chase down, at the cost of their trust.

fields.name: Alberto Gemelli
fields.description: A Naples neighbour of the arrested Signora Esposito-Lau, and Norah Gemelli's husband.
fields.book_role: Part of the circle of friends Lewis builds after that arrest and hopes will outlast the war; when a true leak about the Anzio landing is traced to a dinner at the Gemellis', Lewis is ordered back to pump his own friends for more.

fields.name: Carlo Del Giudice
fields.description: A non-practising Naples lawyer scraping a living writing newspaper articles on folklore and astronomy, and an expert on San Gennaro and Vesuvius.
fields.book_role: Introduced by Lattarullo during the 1944 eruption; he quizzes Lewis about the threatened towns, supplies much of the book's San Gennaro lore, and later joins the parade of eccentric visitors to Lewis's hospital bed.

fields.name: Susanna
fields.description: Lola's friend — 'a frisky redhead of about twenty-five' with an unusually expressive mime.
fields.book_role: A fixture of the Frazer–Lola circle, from the Capri outing to the dinner in the looted flat, where she memorably calls a drunk, boorish British adjutant a cornuto and a stronzo to his uncomprehending face.

fields.name: Contessa della Peruta
fields.description: A beautiful, refined aristocrat living in a near-castle above Santa Maria della Colombina.
fields.book_role: The subject of an 'extraordinary' marriage vetting: the elegance turns out to be staged with borrowed furniture in an otherwise empty house — a sharp variation on the genteel poverty Lewis keeps meeting.

fields.name: Domenico 'Lupo' (Wolf)
fields.description: A young, handsome, dashing bandit of Frattamaggiore — robber of the rich and giver to the poor.
fields.book_role: Freed from prison by the advancing Allies, he rebuilds his band with a forged AMG travel pass; Lewis watches, as an onlooker, the police operation that finally takes him, sprung by his jealous mistress.

fields.name: Fortuna
fields.description: A well-connected penicillin racketeer, a lieutenant of Vito Genovese.
fields.book_role: Lewis visits him in Poggio Reale and finds him serenely certain of acquittal despite the evidence — and he is proved right: an emblem of how the powerful stay 'beyond the reach of the law' while petty thieves rot in the cells.

fields.name: Cuoca
fields.description: The last of the great Camorra chieftains, a figure of the 1920s.
fields.book_role: His end is told on Lewis's tourist day at Pozzuoli: deposed by his own underlings, he was feasted and embraced at a 'funeral feast' at Vicenzo a Mare, then taken away and stabbed to death.

fields.name: George Hankin
fields.description: The one member of the section, Lewis reckons, with 'deep religious scruples'.
fields.book_role: Lands the delicate job of escorting a female internee — too important to be named in writing — to Rome; predictably, she spends the night in prison.

fields.name: Salvatore Loreto
fields.description: A notorious infiltrator and saboteur with the Italian 10th Flotilla MAS.
fields.book_role: Lewis finds him dying in the PW ward at Cancello, shot clean through the body; mistaken for his brother, Loreto throws his arms round Lewis's neck and rambles about their shared childhood as he dies.

fields.name: Giuseppina
fields.description: A 'begrimed and bedraggled' twelve-year-old orphan in Benevento who lives 'under a house' by the river.
fields.book_role: The first abandoned girl Lewis has seen among the city's hundreds of boy-orphans; she comes matter-of-factly to the office to collect her weekly blanket — a currency worth a factory-worker's wage.

fields.name: The Marchesa
fields.description: The last of one of the great landowning families near Benevento — 'laden with jewellery, yellowed with fever', and smoking a pipe.
fields.book_role: Living in her ruined castle among pigeon droppings — selling pigeons to the hotel, growing vegetables in soil spread on the banqueting-hall floor — she boasts of her family's feudal oppressions and turns up, unabashed, at Lewis's supper for the Benevento elite.

fields.name: Marshal Altamura
fields.description: The SIM secret-police officer who effectively runs Benevento — 'handsome, good-humoured, quite imperturbable' and exuding 'sinister power'.
fields.book_role: Ordered by Naples to place himself at Lewis's disposal, he stage-manages Lewis's introduction to the town's notables; but an anonymous letter, and the wounding of Durham, leave Lewis increasingly uneasy that the Marshal is in league with the bandits.

fields.name: Don Ubaldo
fields.description: The schoolmaster of the Benevento town, nominally on the rolls of a left-wing party.
fields.book_role: Gives Lewis the long historical view of Southern Italian banditry — that the bands surface whenever order collapses and attach themselves to the landowners. He dies of typhoid, and the section moves on to Sagranella.

fields.name: Bernard Durham
fields.description: A sergeant in Lewis's Field Security section. (Also recorded here as 'Durham'.)
fields.book_role: Shot through the shoulder by a bandit dressed as an American officer during an anti-bandit drive near Avellino — the section's first casualty.

fields.name: De Micco
fields.description: A farmer in the Benevento countryside.
fields.book_role: Arrested for sheltering a wounded bandit; the arrest draws open disapproval — 'Who wouldn't have done the same thing?' — and marks the point at which the town turns cool toward Lewis.

fields.name: Neil Armstrong
fields.description: A Field Security colleague Lewis last saw in Tunisia eighteen months before.
fields.book_role: Their September 1944 reunion in Benevento — Armstrong now so wary that Lewis half-expects him to grope for his testicles at the sight of a stranger — becomes the book's measure of how completely the south changes a man.

fields.name: Ingeniere Crespi
fields.description: A prosperous Naples engineer, a contact since the Anzio-leak affair.
fields.book_role: Hosts the family mushroom- and bird-hunting expedition to the Lago di Patria that gives the book its portrait of the Neapolitan ottobrate outing.

fields.name: Madonna of Pompeii
fields.description: The Pontifical Shrine of the Blessed Virgin of the Rosary of Pompei is a Catholic cathedral, Marian pontifical shrine, and Pontifical minor basilica commissioned and co-founded by Bartolo Longo and his wife the Countess Mariana di Fusco, located in Pompei, Italy. It is the see of the Territorial Prelature of Pompei.
fields.book_role: A soldier gives Lewis a scrap of tinsel torn from her mantle, promising it will render him bulletproof for a year.

fields.name: evil eye
fields.description: The evil eye is a supernatural belief in a curse brought about by a malevolent glare, usually inspired by envy. Amulets to protect against it have been found dating to around 5,000 years ago. It is found in many cultures in the Mediterranean region, the Balkans, Eastern Europe, West Asia, Central Asia, South Asia, Africa, the Caribbean, and Latin America, with such cultures often believing that receiving the evil eye will cause misfortune or injury, while others believe it to be a kind of supernatural force that casts or reflects a malevolent gaze back upon those who wish harm upon others.
fields.book_role: The pervasive Neapolitan dread of the malevolent glance — coral-horn amulets in every jeweller's window, a Via Carducci block shunned as cursed, a woman blamed for poisoning a village water supply — and, by September 1944, the Benevento notables making protective gestures at Lewis himself, taking him for a jettatore.

fields.name: San Gennaro
fields.description: Januarius, also known as Januarius I of Benevento, was Bishop of Benevento and is a martyr and saint of the Catholic Church. While no contemporary sources on his life are preserved, later sources and legends say he died during the Great Persecution, which ended with Diocletian's retirement in 305.
fields.book_role: The patron of Naples, whose dried blood is expected to liquefy on his feast days; the wartime vigils over whether — and how fast — the miracle happens run through the book as a barometer of public nerves, and his rivalry with San Sebastiano flares during the eruption, when his image is smuggled to San Sebastiano 'on an outside chance'.

fields.name: Zio di Roma
fields.description: A hired mourner who impersonates a distinguished 'uncle from Rome' at a funeral to raise the bereaved family's standing.
fields.book_role: Lattarullo's suspended sideline, resumed once Rome falls — complete with a rented car and driver and a special 'Zio di Roma' suit.

fields.name: San Rocco
fields.description: Roch, also called Rock in English, was a Majorcan Catholic confessor whose death is commemorated on 16 August and 9 September in Italy; he was especially invoked against the plague.
fields.book_role: Advising the exhausted Captain Frazer, Lewis recommends a medal of San Rocco — 'patron of coitus reservatus' — to be had in any religious-supplies shop.

fields.name: Hunchbacks as luck-bringers
fields.description: A Neapolitan belief that a hunched back brings good fortune.
fields.book_role: Lewis notes lottery-ticket buyers touching or stroking a hunchback's hump as part of the purchase.

fields.name: Stork veneration
fields.description: A Southern Italian taboo against harming storks, held to bring bad luck.
fields.book_role: A village that ate its storks' young during the famine is regarded as having called down calamity on itself.

fields.name: Professional wailers
fields.description: Mourners paid to weep and lament at a funeral, amplifying the family's display of loss.
fields.book_role: Lewis notes 'several professional wailers in attendance' at the funeral of a Carabiniere murdered by bandits at Casoria.

fields.name: Blessed Egideo
fields.description: A holy figure whose preserved body is venerated at the church of San Pasquale in Naples.
fields.book_role: The incorrupt body Lewis views in its two-hundred-year-old glass case — serene 'to the point of indifference' — locally famous as the protector of pregnant women, and two miracles short of full sainthood.

fields.name: San Gaetano
fields.description: Gaetano dei Conti di Thiene, known in English as Saint Cajetan, was an Italian Catholic priest and religious reformer, co-founder of the Theatines. He is recognised as a saint in the Catholic Church, and his feast day is 7 August.
fields.book_role: Invoked as a 'powerful exorcist': the remedy for a Via Carducci block of flats blighted by suicides would be for the neighbours to club together and build a street shrine under his protection.

fields.name: Vendetta mourning ritual
fields.description: A funeral rite of the Southern Italian interior in which the dead man's mother mouths his wounds as a pledge of revenge.
fields.book_role: When a man is killed in a vendetta his mother, if living, kisses and sucks at his wounds at the funeral — the kind of 'Bronze-Age' custom Lattarullo, ten miles away in Naples, knows nothing of.

fields.name: pazzariello
fields.description: A traditional Neapolitan costumed figure, part street-advertiser, part exorcist; 'one is born a pazzariello, not made one'.
fields.book_role: Cocked hat, stick, drummers and piper, hired to caper into a newly reopening shop — explained as advertising for the illiterate, but 'his real function is that of an exorcist', driving out evil spirits and the evil eye. Lewis sees his first on the Via San Pasquale.

fields.name: San Sebastiano
fields.description: Sebastian was an early Christian saint and martyr. According to traditional belief, he was killed during the Diocletianic Persecution of Christians. He was initially tied to a post or tree and shot with arrows, though this did not kill him.
fields.book_role: The patron of the town in the lava's path; his processional image is carried out to confront the 1944 eruption, and the smuggling-in of a rival San Gennaro image has to be hidden under a sheet to avoid giving him offence.

fields.name: Sant'Antonio Abate
fields.description: Anthony the Great was a Christian monk from Egypt, revered since his death as a saint. He is distinguished from other saints named Anthony, such as Anthony of Padua, by various epithets: Anthony of Egypt, Anthony the Abbot, Anthony of the Desert, Anthony the Anchorite, Anthony the Hermit, and Anthony of Thebes. For his importance among the Desert Fathers and to all later Christian monasticism, he is also known as the Father of All Monks.
fields.book_role: During the eruption he briefly displaces San Gennaro as the saint charged with holding back Vesuvius's fire.

fields.name: Santo Agnello
fields.description: A Naples church, site of a 'speaking crucifix' during the 1944 miracle fervour.
fields.book_role: Its crucifix carries on a running dialogue with the image of Santa Maria d'Intercessione — reported daily in the newspapers of spring 1944.

fields.name: Santa Maria d'Intercessione
fields.description: A venerated Marian image in Naples.
fields.book_role: In the church of Santo Agnello her image holds a 'regular conversation' with a speaking crucifix — 'a fact confirmed by reporters on the spot' — among the talking, bleeding, sweating images multiplying across Naples in spring 1944.

fields.name: Santa Maria del Carmine
fields.description: Santa Maria del Carmine is a church in Naples, Italy. It is at one end of Piazza Mercato, the centre of civic life in Naples for many centuries until it was cut off from the rest of the city by urban renewal in 1900. The church was founded in the 13th century by Carmelite friars driven from the Holy Land in the Crusades, presumably arriving in the Bay of Naples aboard Amalfitan ships.
fields.book_role: Her image, first said to have bowed its head to dodge a cannon-shot during Alfonso of Aragon's siege of Naples, now 'does this as a matter of daily routine' in the 1944 wave of miracles.

fields.name: St John / San Giovanni a Carbonara
fields.description: A Naples church holding a blood relic said to liquefy.
fields.book_role: One of the churches whose blood relic is reported to be bubbling amid the spring 1944 miracle fever.

fields.name: Sant'Aspreno
fields.description: Aspren or Asprenas was a 1st-century Christian saint and venerated as the first Bishop of Naples.
fields.book_role: The patron invoked against headaches: sufferers push their heads through a hole in the wall of his chapel in search of relief — one of the cures Lewis lists in the miracle-fever of spring 1944.

fields.name: visionary child (local 'Bernadette')
fields.description: A child visionary of the Campi Flegrei reporting Marian apparitions in spring 1944.
fields.book_role: A twelve-year-old girl to whom the Virgin is said to appear with 'comforting messages for the population'; crowds flock out to watch, and the mayor of Marano arrives in a motor-hearse for want of other transport.

fields.name: flying monk of Pomigliano
fields.description: A stigmatic monk of Pomigliano credited with the power of flight — identified in the book's own footnote as the future Padre Pio.
fields.book_role: He claims to have flown through the air to rescue a downed pilot, and displays the stigmata — one of the wave of miracles sweeping the region in 1944.

fields.name: Monte Vergine
fields.description: Sanctuary of Montevergine is a Marian church in Mercogliano, located in the hamlet of Montevergine. It's a part of the Territorial Abbey of Montevergine, one of the six Italian territorial abbeys. Inside, the painting of the Madonna di Montevergine is venerated and it is estimated that about one and a half million pilgrims visit it every year.
fields.book_role: The mountain sanctuary of the Virgin above Avellino, on the site of an ancient shrine of Cybele; the banning of its 1944 Whitsun pilgrimage causes widespread public dismay, and its district furnishes Lattarullo with a lurid tale of fake clergy fleecing a woman black-marketeer.

fields.name: St Michael
fields.description: The Sanctuary of Saint Michael the Archangel is a Roman Catholic shrine on Mount Gargano, Italy, part of the commune of Monte Sant'Angelo, in the province of Foggia, northern Apulia. It has the dignity of a minor basilica.
fields.book_role: The cave-sanctuary at Monte Sant'Angelo in Puglia — source of the venerated lump of rock that is, with a royal salver, the one treasured possession in Lattarullo's bare flat.

fields.name: Parenti di San Gennaro
fields.description: A clique of aged Neapolitan women held to be the blood descendants of San Gennaro.
fields.book_role: Led in to take their places around the cathedral altar, they are credited with the power — and the duty — of browbeating their ancestor into performing the blood miracle.

fields.name: Ischia radioactive cure belief
fields.description: A local conviction that Ischia's natural radioactivity is health-giving.
fields.book_role: The belief that the Naples-facing side of Ischia is beneficially radioactive — slimming, good for the kidneys, bladder and complexion — is why Lola and Susanna go there for the summer 'to deflate'.

fields.name: Guardia Sanframondi flagellant rite
fields.description: Guardia Sanframondi is a town and comune in the Province of Benevento, in Campania region, in Italy. It is best known for its wine production, the wine festival Vinalia and for its Christian penitential rite held every seven years.
fields.book_role: The seven-yearly penitential procession in honour of the Virgin, revived in 1944 — described to Lewis by a colleague: robes soaked with blood, and one banner-carrier nearly lynched after being publicly named a cuckold.

fields.name: Festival of the Lilies (Nola)
fields.description: Paulinus of Nola born Pontius Meropius Anicius Paulinus, was a Roman poet, writer, senator, and bishop. He attained the ranks of suffect consul and governor of Campania, but, prompted by the counsels of his Hispanic wife Therasia of Nola and by the assassination of the emperor Gratian, abandoned his career and was baptized as a Christian. Later, probably after Therasia's death, he became bishop of Nola in Campania.
fields.book_role: Nola's Feast of St Paulinus, in which towering wooden 'lily' structures are carried through the streets; in 1944 the procession brought the town to a standstill and sliced through the army's telephone cables by the hundred — Eric Williams's despair.

fields.name: St Andrew's Manna (Amalfi)
fields.description: Amalfi Cathedral is a medieval Roman Catholic cathedral in the Piazza del Duomo, Amalfi, Italy. It is dedicated to the Apostle Saint Andrew whose relics are kept here. Formerly the archiepiscopal seat of the Diocese of Amalfi, it has been since 1986 that of the Diocese of Amalfi-Cava de' Tirreni.
fields.book_role: The relic in the crypt of Amalfi Cathedral said to exude a miraculous liquid several times a year; Del Giudice asks Lewis to drive him there, and queues to buy a sample.

fields.name: Sagranella fox-cult
fields.description:
While stationed in southern Italy during the war, Lewis came across accounts of "fox-magic" in Sagranella, a remote village located in the hills behind Benevento. 

He noted that the village felt so isolated and archaic that it "seems hardly to have moved out of the Bronze Age."According to his writings, the local cult ritual involved two primary acts:

- The Ritual Sacrifice: Every year, the villagers would capture a live fox and burn it to death.
- The Display: After the burning, the fox's tail was severed and hung like a banner from a pole erected at the entrance of the village.

Historians and travel writers often link this specific practice to ancient Samnite or localized pagan traditions in the region, where animals were sacrificed to ward off evil spirits, ensure agricultural fertility, or mark territory.
fields.book_role: The annual ritual of the hill village where the section is billeted after Don Ubaldo's death: a live fox burned to death and its tail hung 'like a banner' from a pole at the village entrance, near an Easter Island-style stone head probably older than the Samnites.

fields.name: Droit du seigneur (Sagranella)
fields.description: The lord's claimed right of sexual access to the women of his estate.
fields.book_role: Said, at Sagranella, to be still practised as a matter of course on the neighbouring big estate, whose steward reportedly feels a prospective woman worker's muscles before hiring her for a sixteen-hour day.

fields.name: fertility offering superstition
fields.description: A gesture read as a survival of ancient fertility worship.
fields.book_role: A woman's ritual gesture that Lewis takes for an offering to a fertility deity — one of the glimpses of pre-Christian cult he keeps catching in and around Naples.

fields.summary: Aboard ship off Italy, news arrives of the armistice; Lewis notes the total lack of intelligence about what awaits them at Salerno.
Landing at Paestum amid dead soldiers and eerie calm; the section is left rudderless, with no briefing, next to the ancient temples.
A strafing run and near-miss becomes almost routine; Lewis contrasts his own hardened nerves with the panic of green American troops.
HQ moves to a tranquil rural setting, but there's a creeping sense that the Fifth Army is unprepared and undefended.
A German counterattack triggers real chaos — panicked tank crews, gas scares, and rumours that Mark Clark may abandon the beachhead.
An intense night battle near the beachhead, with naval bombardment lighting the sky and hurried, ad hoc arming of the intelligence men.
A comrade's harrowing return from Salerno; confusion persists as officers and men lose track of each other amid ongoing shelling.
